utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Today we are Monday, 28th of January, 2008. I would like to greet all the representatives of the Prosecution. I see that there's a few of them. And I would like to say hello also to the Defence teams, as well as to the accused. And I see and notice that they're all present. I would also like to greet the interpreters, the usher, the registrar as well as our legal officers. Before this hearing according to Rule 98 bis begins, there are a few decisions that the Chamber will render orally. First I would like to mention to the parties that as I'm speaking to you, we are registering the decision with regard to the request of delays for the Prosecution case. This decision, which is made of ten pages, approximately, will be brought to your knowledge, but I would just like to tell you what it is going to be about, major points that you raised. We have decided to modify the schedule which was initially made in this way: The lists of witnesses and of exhibits that will have to be filed by 31st of March, 2008. The Pre-Trial Conference is to take place on the 21st of April, 2008, and the resumption of the hearing of the Defence witnesses will start as of Monday, 5 May, 2008. In the meantime during that period, we are going to hold two hearings, pre-trial hearings. They are already on the schedule. On the 10th and 26th of March, 2008. So to sum is up, the resumption will take place on the 5th of May, 2008. This being said, I am going to deal with other decisions regarding other issues. And now a decision regarding a translation matter. On the 24th of January, 2008, the Accused Praljak filed a motion to the Chamber requesting that the Chamber orders the Registry to ease the translation process or to help them in the translation process. The Chamber requests that the Registrar files in writing his comments under article -- Rule 33(B) of the Rules before the 11th of February, 2008, at the latest. Second oral decision pertaining to the raising of the private session for transcripts during the hearing of the 24th of January, 2008. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution ended the presentation of their case at the end of the hearing of the 24th of January, 2008, while the Court was still in private session. The witness who testified that day or his appearance does not justify that the transcript be under -- in private session, and the Chamber decides according to Rule 81(B) that it will lift the private session for the French transcript on pages 26867, line 17, all the way to page 26868, line 22. Third point: This point regards the issue that took place regarding the time given to Ms. Alaburic during the cross-examination of Witness DZ last Thursday. There was a disagreement on the time remaining for Ms. Alaburic to carry the cross-examination of the witness. After calculating the time, the registry informed the Chamber that there was in fact 13 minutes left for Ms. Alaburic, whereas the Chamber had told her that she had no time left. The Chamber therefore notices that there was a mistake made on that issue. The Chamber therefore would like to say that it is unfortunate, but since we worked under conditions which were such as we worked all very fast there was a mistake in the calculation, and you still have 13 minutes left. This is what I wanted to tell Ms. Alaburic and Mr. Stewart. Fourth point, oral decision relating to the request by Accused Praljak to take the floor. During the hearing of the 24th of January, 2008, the Defence of the Accused Praljak requested the Chamber to allow the Accused Praljak to take the floor in order to make his submissions on a certain number of questions when it comes to oral arguments filed under Rule 98 bis of the Rules. The Chamber notes that in the meantime the Defence of the Accused Praljak informed the Chamber by e-mail that it will -- they will not make oral arguments according to Rule 98 bis of the Rules but that the accused would nevertheless like to take the floor. The Chamber reminds the Accused Praljak that the Statute and the Rules are the ones making the procedure and the Rule states very precisely and clearly when the accused can take the floor and address the Chamber. The procedure under Rule 98 bis of the Rules pertains to acquittal requests and not to accused's statements. Since the Accused Praljak does not wish to file an acquittal request, his request to take the floor at this stage of the proceeding is rejected. However, the Chamber recalls that an accused may make a statement under Rule 84 bis of the Rules. The Chamber notes that the Accused Praljak already made a statement under this Rule before the beginning of the Prosecution case on the 27th of April, 2006. The Chamber would nevertheless be ready to authorise the Accused Praljak to take the floor once more to make a statement at the time when the Defence is presenting its case. So I will summarise in one word. The Accused Praljak may not intervene during the 98 bis procedure. However, on the 5th of May, 2008, when the hearing resumes, if no general acquittal took place, the Accused Praljak will be able to intervene and to make his statement as a complement to [Realtime transcript read in error "tomorrow"] the submissions and statements that he already made on the 27th of April, 2006. This is what the Chamber wanted to tell General Praljak. Yes. My colleague is telling me that there's a mistake at line 19. I did not say tomorrow, but I said in addition to his statement that he made on the 27th of April, 2006. I do not know why the word "tomorrow" figures in the transcript. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone, to the Trial Chamber and everybody else in the courtroom. I'd like to thank you for the observation made about the time that I had at my disposal, and unfortunately due to force of circumstance I was not able to use. I'd also like to thank your associates who contacted us on Thursday straight away after the mistake was noted and we absolutely do understand that every one of us can make a mistake, and we thank you for the explanation and even the Prosecution has the right to make mistakes, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Ms. Alaburic. It is true it is quite difficult to have an absolute control on time. I would have to have a chronometer or a stopwatch and as soon as somebody starts speaking I press on the button so that the time stops. But normally our registrar is Mr. Stopwatch; he is doing his best but as you know he has lots to do. He has to control what's on the transcript. He also is the one who has to take care of videos and documents to be presented, and he is under a permanent pressure. So it is quite possible that at times some small mistakes can happen. So we're all very well aware of that fact, and we will try in the future to improve the system. Now regarding the procedure of Rule 98 bis, normally three counsels will intervene, counsel for Mr. Petkovic, counsel for Mr. Coric, and counsel for Mr. Pusic. As I see that Ms. Alaburic already prepared her lectern, I will hand the floor to her at this time, and at the end of this phase the Prosecution will be able to reply. Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I apologise for interrupting counsel just as she was get to go her feet or on her feet, but I think it might be an appropriate moment given what's been said in the last few minutes in terms of the time pressures and circumstances which all of us have worked over the past months. And I just want to alert the Chamber now so that there isn't any misunderstanding later. As the Chamber will recall, there's been a great number of evidentiary rulings in the past -- in the past few days. In my experience both in this Tribunal and in my prior practice in the United States, in all but the very smallest cases there has always been an opportunity to -- for the parties, for the registry, and for others to meet to possibly reconcile any -- any errors or oversights that have indeed been made and as we've just seen with the issue of time, in a case of this scope and magnitude and complexity it is quite easy for errors to be made by all parties. I hope no one would be offended by that. Errors by the Prosecution, errors by the Defence, errors by the registry, and indeed errors by the Chamber. It is the nature of this difficult and complicated process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, judges do not make mistakes as a general rule but if you say they make mistakes, well, there is the Appeals Chamber for that. But so far I did not -- I was not under the impression that we made any mistake whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, last time I checked all of you were human and indeed judges do make mistakes, and I stand by my statement. There are items that immediate to be addressed Your Honour. The Prosecution has not had the time yet to look at these matters in preparing for these hearings and closing our case having presented our final witness last week and the matters that have had to be attended to in the immediate days but I do think there are a number of items, Your Honours that will have to -- need to be look at further. I think evidence should be excluded on substantive grounds, not relevant, lack of authentication, lack of foundation, what have you, but evidence should not be excluded based on error or mistake. And I think there are a number of items that the Prosecution when time allows when we complete these 98 bis proceedings will ask to address and I just wanted to inform the Chamber of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours, a very brief comment first of all with Your Honours' leave in relation to the comments put forward by my learned friend Mr. Scott. A distinction must be drawn in my respectful submission between administrative errors and legal mistakes that are alleged by a party. There is no problem at all on the side of counsel for Mr. Stojic, and I believe the Defence speak with one voice that if there are administrative mistakes that can be dealt with without troubling Your Honours with your very capable legal staff, your senior legal officers and your legal officers. If it's alleged by the Prosecution that matters have been excluded in error or matters have been admitted in error, well, that's a completely different kettle of fish. The rules are there about time for appeal. The Prosecution's case is closed, and the Rules are self-explanatory. I don't see how assertions of legal error can be dealt with in an informal manner. Administrative mistakes, exhibit numbers being duplicated are very different and there would not be a problem in relation to that. Your Honour, I did say on behalf of -- we did say on behalf of Mr. Stojic last week that we were not going to make any Rule 98 bis submission. That remains the case. But for the record and for the information of the client, and of course for Your Honours, we do maintain the not guilty plea. We do continue to put the Prosecution to strict proof as is our right on each element of each count of the indictment, and we do look forward to putting forward a defence case that any matters that remain opaque at this moment hopefully can be clarified in our defence case. Your Honour, that's the first point. The second point refers to a submission put forward very eloquently by my learned friend Nicholas Stewart, Queen's Counsel, a couple of weeks back and Your Honours decide that any argument regarding the scope of Rule 98 bis could be made in the submissions of particular counsel. Your Honour, what counsel for the co-accused, at least Mr. Stewart, is going to do, and he did indicate and forewarn Your Honours of his position, is that if a count -- if Your Honours find that there is sufficient evidence taken at its highest, that a reasonable Tribunal could convict on a count, the count could proceed but nonetheless Your Honours could red-line particular paragraphs of that count. I think that's the thrust of the submission that my learned friend is going to make. Your Honours, I'm not going to address you on that unless you think it helpful but in the event that Your Honours are persuaded in relation to that submission, it stands to reason and as a matter of fairness, in my respectful submission, that any paragraphs that are struck out, notwithstanding that the count remains, should benefit all accused equally. I think that's a very logical and basic principle. Your Honour, those are my very brief comments. I don't know if they help clarify the matters but I thought it important to put them down on the record in any event. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Two observations. Regarding the mistakes, it is obvious that administrative mistakes can be corrected without any problem, as you stated, if in decision or motions some confusion took place as to exhibit numbers or other. This can, of course, be corrected very easily. However, if the Prosecution maintains that some legal mistakes took place and requests reconsideration on those, it will, of course, be looked at with a magnifying glass, because under the Rule when a decision is rendered the parties have a certain number of days to present a certification for appeal, and if that is not done it is over. So I don't know what the Prosecution wanted to mention. If these are administrative mistakes of course there is no problem whatsoever. The necessary corrections will be made. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I really didn't mean to invite a great discussion of this today. I thought it might be helpful and proper for me simply to advise the Chamber that we had those concerns and would be seeking to address them. I certainly did not mean to get off into these matters and derail the 98 bis proceedings today. I'm not going to at this point characterise further any particular type of error that may have been made. I do think that there are a number that could be considered to be clerical, administrative, a result of confusion, et cetera, on all -- on potentially different sides. And I'm not alleging any bad faith nor do I think any bad faith should be directed at the Prosecution. We're all here trying to do a difficult job. We all come from different legal cultures, Your Honour, and I think in a system in which there are different languages are spoken, different legal concepts are used, different -- there's different legal backgrounds, that sometimes there is an honest -- among other things and I'm not saying -- I'm just saying among other things, there is an honest misunderstanding. There are honest mistakes on various sides and I don't think those kinds of misunderstandings and mistakes should be the basis for the exclusion of evidence for any party, Prosecution or Defence. And I simply thought it was prudent, Your Honour, and fair to the Chamber and everyone to simply indicate when we have the time there are certain matters we believe do need to be addressed. And as I said a few moments ago, in my experience here in the last ten years and in my prior experience in the United States in all but the simplest cases where one might have 10 exhibits in the case there is a process by which these sorts of verifications and checking is done. It was done in the Kordic case; it was done in the Tuta and Stela case; and it is standard practice in my experience. And that is the only thing that I am raising to the Chamber's attention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I could I just raise one matter if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A slight concern, Your Honour. It does appear that the basis on which Your Honours have rejected Mr. Praljak's application seems to imply a view on the very issue which I raised a few days ago on an application for preliminary issue and Your Honours expressed the view that it was at least an issue to be explored on this application as to whether the ambit of Rule 98 bis went beyond acquittal on an entire count; and yet the thrust of your rejection -- I'm not standing here for Mr. Praljak, but I'm just concerned about the implications of Your Honours' decision on his application for where we stand and would seek Your Honours' assurance that -- that there is no degree of pre-emption and that issue does remain live. It's actually my legal lead counsel who is going to argue that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's see what comes out, but in the mind of the Trial Chamber, 98 bis is 98 bis and not anything else. So there's absolutely nothing else to say on this Rule. However, if an accused wishes to intervene at this stage of the procedure, he may do so under Rule 84 bis which -- 98 bis, correction, which brings us to Rule 84 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We have been speaking of misunderstandings. I think it's important to set two misunderstandings right here. The first one is the question of whether Mr. Praljak takes the floor or not is totally unrelated to the question of whether we examine arguments per count or even per charge. So I see no relation there whatsoever. On the other hand, you have, Mr. Stewart, made a hint at a possibility which we said we might perhaps -- I said that perhaps it might be considered. I was sort of expecting a more formal motion from you which has not since appeared. The Chamber has discussed the issue, and the Chamber has been quite firm that it is not of the opinion that it has the competency, according to the present law applied in this court, to decide on anything else but on counts. So it's either a count is -- leads to an acquittal or not, but the Chamber will not look at single charges. And one of the reasons is rather obvious, because if we were doing that we would have to expect arguments on every charge, which would by far exceed the scope of the 98 bis proceedings as they are actually handled in this court. I wanted to make this clear, and I'm sorry if there has been a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's not my personal opinion; that is the result of discussions with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I understand that, Your Honour, and when a view is expressed on behalf of all three of Your Honours it's even more helpful than having individual views expressed by individual Judges that may or may not coincide with the views of others. Your Honour, as far as the substance of the matter is concerned, I'm certainly not going to tread on the toes of my learned lead counsel; she is going to deal with that issue. But I am slightly, I've used the word troubled I think twice today, I'm slightly troubled about what Your Honour said about expecting some sort of formal motion from us because without having the transcript of what happened on my application preliminary issue in front of me, I do have a distinct recollection that the upshot of it was that Your Honours made it clear that it was to be open to us on this hearing to raise that particular issue, which is entirely inconsistent with the notion that we were to file some sort of formal motion. And in fact, Your Honour, may I simply also observe that the whole point of my application for the matter to be dealt with as a preliminary issue was to give that some formality as a separate discrete issue. So, Your Honour, I must say with respect that if it is now suggested that in some way we might have failed or our position might be weakened by not filing a formal motion, then I must protest that, frankly, innocently though it may be we would have been quite seriously misled by the procedure indicated by the Trial Chamber. Honestly misled, of course, we do not bandy about any allegations of dishonesty or bad faith on this side of the case in the Petkovic team, but that will have been the effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall listen carefully to what Defence counsel have to say. Mrs. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of General Petkovic would like to remind the Trial Chamber that a few days ago it tabled an oral request for a special discussion to be organised with respect to the application of Rule 98 bis, because they considered that with respect to certain questions, we can decide upon this as prejudicial issues and that this would help us in setting forth the 98 bis submissions. The Court ruling was that a separate debate would not be organised but that the Petkovic Defence within its frameworks of its submission pursuant to Rule 98 bis could set forth arguments and the grounds for a different interpretation of the application of Rule 98 bis and possibly to request that the proceedings be conducted differently than they are being today. Now, precisely for this reason the Defence of General Petkovic has structured its submission on 92 -- 98 bis in three parts. It has set it out in three parts. The first part will refer to the existence of current case law and jurisprudence and an interpretation of Rule 98 bis, and this part of the submission will be presented by me. In continuation, we're going to try, depending on the Court ruling on the previous issues that we're going to initiate in the introductory part will be tabled according to Rule 98 bis as the text now stands with an interpretation of the fact that it is possible to bring in judgements of acquittal on the individual parts or counts of the indictment. The third part would refer to an earlier submission of ours from last year when we requested that certain forms of criminal responsibility be struck from the indictment and the Trial Chamber ruling was that it would make its final decision and ruling in the proceedings on Rule 98 bis. Now, the second part of our submission will be presented orally by my colleague Mr. Nicholas Stewart and part 3 which relates to striking certain forms of criminal responsibilities will be expounded by myself. Let us start off by the application and interpretation of Rule 98 bis in the text as it reads and exists today and this can be considered a preliminary issue. With your permission, Your Honours, and with the permission of my colleagues in the courtroom, I'd like to start off by making a few introductory remarks on the -- on human rights and what they are based on as the starting point for the application and interpretation of the laws. The first basic human right which in all criminal proceedings appears is the presumption of innocence. It is the right that we have heard mentioned frequently in this trial. We all know its contents. We all know its meaning, but let me remind you of some of the basic elements there. We are dealing with a right that is guaranteed by Article 11 of the general declaration on human rights and Article 6, paragraph 2, of the European Convention on Human Rights, but also the rights guaranteed by all other international contracts and covenants on human rights and freedoms as well as the constitutions of all countries. The contents of that right is that a person who stands accused of a crime is considered innocent until guilt has been proved in conformity with the regulations. So guilt -- the burden is proof is on the Prosecution. If the Prosecution is unable to prove guilt then the accused must be acquitted of all criminal responsibility. The continuation of the criminal proceedings, despite the fact that the Prosecution has failed to prove the accused's guilt is a violation of a basic human right which is the right of the presumption of innocence. In other words, to acquit an accused because the Prosecutor has not managed to prove guilt is the direct consequence of the recognition and respect of human rights and the presumption of innocence principle. The acquittal of an accused because the Prosecutor has not proved guilt also fulfils a second human right, that is to say, the right to a fair trial. The arguments a contrario, that is to say, a trial which leads the accused -- brings the accused into a situation to defend himself from a charge which has not been proved becomes unfair. By continuing the legal proceedings despite the fact that the Prosecutor has not managed to prove the guilt of the accused, we violate the third basic human right which is the right to a trial within a reasonable space of time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak louder into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that reason, the presumption of innocence, the right to a fair trial and the right to a trial within a set period of time, an expeditious and speedy trial, are basic concerns -- let me repeat. I'm sorry, I'm not listening to the interpretation so I apologize for speeding up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak louder, please, into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the presumption of innocence and the right to a fair trial and the right to be tried expeditiously within a given period of time is the basic concern of those creating the Rules of Procedure of a criminal trial. But it is also the basic concern of those applying the Rules of Procedure in a criminal trial, and it is also the starting point in interpreting and applying rights. If some rule of proceeding in a criminal trial or the application of those rules of procedure violates basic human rights and freedoms such as the presumption of innocence, the right to a fair trial, and the right to an expeditious trial within a reasonable period of time, that -- it is the task of every Defence counsel to indicate these violations and to initiate steps to do away with this violation. The importance of the questions being put forward and with arguments through which it brings out its presentation the Defence counsel contributes to the development of case law and jurisprudence and law in general not only in the common law countries but also in the countries of so-called continental law. Trial Chambers are ready to interpret and apply the horizons of these rules in different ways and extend jurisprudence, show that right is not a dogma but that it is an effective means for bringing to life and protecting human rights and freedoms. This same legal norm can be interpreted -- I would like to repeat the beginning of the sentence. That this same legal norm can be applied and interpreted in numerous ways. That it can be applied in numerous ways there are many examples and it is enough to remember the Supreme Court of the USA which for over 200 years in interpreting the same text of the constitution creates the right which is the same law which is adapted to changes in social relations and this is something that happens in other countries too. Examples of this can be found there not only in the United States of America. I hope you won't mind me having made that extensive introduction, but I will try to bring those basic human rights in due course in line and in connection with the -- with Rule 98 bis and the way it is applied to the present day. Now I'd like to say a few words about Rule 98 bis itself. This Rule in the text as adopted on the 8th of December, 2004 reads as follows: "At the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." The previous text of Rule 98 bis that was in force, instead of the count of any count, that is use the term "criminal act" or "charge" in English. And Rule 98 bis read, and I'll read it out in English as follows: "[In English] The Trial Chamber shall order the entry of judgement of acquittal if it finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on that or those charges." [Interpretation] Your Honours of the Trial Chamber, I'd like to inform you that the Defence of General Petkovic is acquainted with case law as it has been applied according to Rule 98 bis, that we have studied the decisions from the Milutinovic and other trials, Mrksic et al., Krajisnik trial and so on, and with your permission we would like to summarise the jurisprudence or case law and then we will say that according to that case law there are eight basic premises for a judgement of acquittal to be passed, and the first is this: If there is not -- no evidence which supports a specific count in the indictment. Second, if there are certain -- if there is a certain amount of evidence and the Defence claims that on the basis of that proof and evidence a judgement of acquittal cannot be moved, then the decision pursuant to Rule 98 bis does not depend on the question of whether the person bringing in the judgement in this phase of the proceedings moved a judgement of acquittal or found the accused guilty. What is -- it is not that we are testing whether the Prosecutor has proved beyond reasonable doubt the guilt of the accused. The legal standard is far lower and requires an examination into whether evidence and proof exists on the basis of which a reasonable trier of the case would be convinced beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused pursuant to a specific indictment. If the reasonable trier is not convinced of the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, then he must pass a judgement of acquittal. The third element is this: The probative value -- if the probative value of certain testimonies by witnesses or documents is not tested; in other words, if the contradictions and inconsistencies of the Prosecution case are not tested and investigated and the credibility of the witness, reliability, and probative value of the documents presented. And the fourth presumption: If the only relevant piece of evidence is so lacks credibility that it could not support the indictment even if the biggest weight could be assigned to this piece of evidence, the motion on Rule 98 bis would be granted. The fifth presumption: A judgement of acquittal pertains to a count in the indictment and not to any specific crime or charge. Six: If one count of an indictment covers two or more crimes, in order for a judgement of acquittal to be entered, all the presumptions regarding every crime in a single count of the indictment have to be met. Seven: The evidence relates both to the actus reus and to the mens rea of each specific crime. Eight: If the indictment or a charge covers several forms of criminal responsibility, it is enough that evidence exists to support the conviction on just one of those forms of responsibility. To sum up, I think that everybody in the courtroom would agree with the following conclusion: Rule 98 bis, as it stands now, seen in light of the jurisprudence, existing jurisprudence, is a mere formality and practically there is no -- it is not possible to enter a judgement of acquittal at this stage of the proceedings. It is a generally held view that such practice before this Tribunal is unfair but that nothing can be changed for as long as Rule 98 bis as formulated in December 2004 is valid, is in force. Let us go back to what was said at the beginning about basic human rights. The conclusion that a rule or a procedure is unfair motivates every lawyer who respects the principle of fairness as the highest value of the legal theory and practice to oppose the continuation of the application of such theory and practice and to try and find a solution that would move the practice forward in the direction of justice and fairness. So we challenge the presumptions six and eight as listed above. In other words, that all the elements have to be met for each single count, and if several forms of criminal responsibility are covered in an indictment, that it is enough to submit evidence to support the conviction on just one form. Let me now give an outline of -- of our case in light of the jurisprudence in the world. First of all, what is a count in an indictment? Is it whatever is designated as such by the Prosecution in the indictment, or are there any objective criteria for formulating counts in the indictment? Furthermore, does the Prosecution formulate the counts of the indictment in the same manner for all the accused before this Tribunal, and if this is not the case, does it then discriminate against some of the accused making their defence more difficult and relieving some of them of the right to a fair trial? I think that all of us lawyers in this courtroom will agree that there are several basic rules of criminal procedure before international and national courts alike. The first rule is that the Court and the parties may proceed only in accordance with the rules. Second, the Court and the parties may do so in the manner that is defined by the rules; and third, whatever is not envisaged and permitted by the Rules of Procedure cannot be done in the course of the proceedings. Are there any rules in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal as to what counts in the indictment are and how they may or must be formulated? It is uncontroversial that a single count in the indictment may cover a single incident, a single event, a single crime. This is a single incident count. This is not controversial before this Tribunal, but is it possible for a single count in the indictment to cover several incidents, several events? In other words, do the Rules of this Tribunal allow for multi-incident counts, counts that cover several charges within a single count? We will try to find this out as we proceed. Let us first refer to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and let us now try to analyse some of the counts in the indictment. If you read the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we will find that the Rules recognise only two kinds of joinder, joinder of counts within a single indictment, that is Rule 49, which reads: "A single indictment can include two or several crimes if they are committed together as part of the same transaction and if the said crimes were committed by the same accused." This Rule undoubtedly shows that the indictment must cover a single crime and exceptionally, and the criteria are defined here, several crimes may be covered. The second kind of joinder that is recognised by the Rules is the joinder of accused as stipulated in Rule 48, which is not the focus of our interest at this moment. The term "joinder" is again mentioned in Rule 72(A)(iii), which deals with preliminary motions where it says: "[In English] Preliminary motions being motions which seek the severance of counts joined in one indictment under Rule 49." [Interpretation] If we compare these two provisions, we will see that the term "crime" as used in Rule 49 is synonymous with the term "count" as used in Rule 72(A)(iii). There is no mention of the possibility of having several counts, several crimes, within a single count of the indictment. The only logical conclusion is that several crimes may be joined in a single indictment, but it is not possible to join several crimes within a single count of the indictment. Your Honours, let me now go back to make some parallels about the concurrence of crimes and the joinder of crimes in some other countries. Trials for multiple crimes is something that is called a real concurrence. It is a legal institution whereby several crimes are committed in the course of several acts, and the accused are tried in a single trial. There is also the ideal concurrence where a single -- where several crimes were committed in a single act. Because of the similarities in the contents of the indictments, I think it would be much more a posit for us to look to common law countries when it comes to the issue of joinder of counts. I would like to refer to law -- case law in Great Britain and the United States. And according to criminal procedure rules in Great Britain, the rules that were adopted in 2005, the rule is that a single count in the indictment covers only one incident. Only in exceptional cases, if all the conditions that are very precisely defined have been met, a single count in the indictment can cover several incidents. Article 14.2.2 of the British law: "[In English] More than one incident of the commission of the events may be included in a count if those incidents taken together amount to a course of conduct having regard to the time, place, or purpose of commission." [Interpretation] The regulation entitled the consolidated Criminal Practice Direction, Chapter 4, Article 34(8) through (12), it is stipulated when it is permissible to cover two or more incidents in a single count. And this directive stipulates quite clearly that the alternatives are either to have multiple incident crimes or to have a separate count, multiple incident counts, so not -- not crimes. I have to correct myself. The alternatives are multiple incident counts or to have a separate count for each incident. A second example, Canada. The Canadian Criminal Code, in paragraphs 581 through 591, indicates: "Each count in an indictment shall in general apply to a single transaction and shall contain in substance a statement that the accused or defendant committed an offence therein specified." [Interpretation] A count in the indictment that covers two or more incidents is considered to be a joinder of counts. So that's what we're talking about. And there is a very important rule in Canada. The accused has the right at every stage in the proceedings to demand a severance of the count that contains several incidents if the joinder of the counts made his defence more difficult or -- I will now just give you another example from the USA. Section 585 of the Criminal Code says: "A single indictment may be used to indict a person only of a single crime only in the following three -- except in the following three cases: "[In English] Where several distinct indictable offences form or are part of a series of offences of the same or similar character; drugo, where several distinct indictable offences are alleged to be constituted by the same acts or omissions; trece, where several distinct indictable offences are alleged to have been done or omitted for a single purpose." [Interpretation] So the condition for the joinder -- there are conditions and rules that regulate the issue of joinder. What is the reason for the restrictions to the joinder of the counts or charges? It is quite clear, and let me read it out: "[In English] The restriction upon joinder of charges stems from the fundamental principle that evidence of the commission of offences other than the offence charged is generally inadmissible against the defendant at a criminal trial. Allowing evidence of other offences may unjustly erode the presumption of innocence which underlies all criminal trials." [Interpretation] To conclude, any joinder, not only of several crimes within a single indictment but also of several crimes within a single count of the indictment, is allowed only if the regulations envisage that and in the manner that is envisaged. The rules of this Tribunal do not envisage that several crimes or charges can be subsumed within the same or joined within the same count. Let us now try and analyse the indictments that were drafted by the Office of the Prosecutor and to compare the rights of the accused in light of the way in which the counts of the indictment were actually drafted. Let us look first at the following topic: One kind of a crime in several counts of the indictment. We all know that our indictment was drafted in such a way that every count contains a specific kind of a crime, and then it covers all the incidents that in the view of the Prosecution present the commission of this crime. If we compare our indictment with the indictments in other cases, we will see what happened, for instance, in the Dusko Tadic case. The Dusko Tadic indictment contained 34 counts. One crime. I will now be given -- giving just the reference in the Statute so as not to waste time. So crimes listed in Article 2(c) of the Statute were described in seven counts; Article 3 in six counts; inhumane acts, Article 5(i) of the Statute in seven counts, and so on. A second example, the Kunarac and Kovac case. Kunarac and Kovac. 25 counts, some more examples. Crime of rape, Article 5(g) of the Statute was contained in six counts of the indictment. Torture, Article 3 of the Statute, was covered in two counts of the indictment, and so on. A third example, Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case. The crime of murder, Article 3, two counts of the indictment. Cruel treatment, Article 3, two counts of the indictment. Why is this important at all, and why am I comparing those counts? For the following reason: If a single count in the indictment covers one incident or just a few incidents, then the accused, in light of the current case law, has -- stands a greater chance of being acquitted on Rule 98 bis. The indictments that are drafted in such a way that one kind of a crime is covered in several counts of the indictment by its very nature each count contains a smaller number of incidents than would have been the case if a single count covers all the incidents of the same kind. In this case the accused, who have been charged on count -- several counts of the indictment, have a greater chance of succeeding under Article -- under Rule 98 bis. The conclusion is that the accused have been discriminated against in comparison with the other cases where not all of the incidents or crimes of the same kind are included in the same count because the Prosecution decided to have several counts containing -- covering crimes of the same kind. It is beyond dispute that the indictment in this case, just as in all other cases, could have been formulated in such a way to make sure that one count of indictment pertained only to one charge, one crime. If we take the position that the Prosecution classified correctly within certain paragraphs all counts, then it would mean that our indictment with single incident counts would have 993 counts. Now let us analyse another topic pertaining to the indictment and the rights of the accused when it comes to the manner in which an indictment is formulated. This other topic pertains to the following issue: Does one count cover one indictee or a number of them? In the Kordic and Cerkez case we saw that there were a total of 44 counts of indictment out of which 22 pertained to Kordic only, and 22 to Cerkez only. Why is this issue important? If according to the existing jurisprudence an acquittal under Rule 98 bis can be handed down only if all the requirements for acquittal are met in relation to each crime from one count. So if an entire count is dismissed, then we have to ask ourselves whether just one accused can be acquitted in relation to that count but that count can remain valid in relation to other accused, or can one accused be acquitted of any count only if at the same time according to the -- to Rule 98 bis all other indictees can be acquitted as well under the same count. This issue is particularly important in the context of joint criminal enterprise and its application here before this Tribunal. The position taken in the jurisprudence that a count of the indictment which pertains to all of the accused can be dropped under Rule 98 bis only if each accused can be acquitted on that charge -- under that charge. If that position were to be taken, that would mean that the accused in this case are even more discriminated against than other accused in whose cases the counts of indictment pertain equally to all of the co-accused. If we wanted to have separate counts of indictment in relation to each -- all of the accused, then the 993 crimes that I have mentioned should be multiplied by six accused, which would mean that we would have an indictment with a total of 5.958 counts of the accused. Now, could the Defence of General Pusic [as interpreted] please forgive me for neglecting the fact that Mr. Pusic [as interpreted] is not charged in relation to the crimes from Prozor in October of 1992 and Gornji Vakuf in January of 1993. Another issue that I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to are the forms of criminal responsibility. It is a rule in the criminal procedure that due to a different actus reus and mens rea each form of perpetration is considered a different crime. For example, issuing an order to commit a crime is one type of a crime. Commission of that crime is another type of a crime. Command responsibility for that same act is yet a third type of a crime. If one person is charged with the same incident due to planning, save from Article 7(1) of the Statute, and is also charged for command responsibility from Article 7(3) of the Statute, then it is clear that that person is charged for two very different crimes. Charging for the same incident under several modes of responsibility and the fact that it actually represents two or several crimes is something that we can see if we look at the application of Rule 98 bis in Blagojevic and Jokic case. The Trial Chamber in that case, in relation to counts 2 to 4 of the indictment, acquitted Mr. Blagojevic with respect to his individual responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. He was acquitted for planning, instigating, ordering, and committing crimes, which means that what he was left with is criminal responsibility under Article 7(3). The Trial Chamber also acquitted Mr. Blagojevic under counts 5 and 6 of the indictment with respect to allegations about his individual responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute for planning, instigating, and ordering commission of crimes, which means that he was left with the allegation of commission under Article 7(1), and commission under Article 7(3). Mr. Jokic was acquitted in relation to counts 2 to 5 of the indictment in terms of his individual responsibility under Article 7(1) for planning, instigating and ordering, and according to the indictment, he was to be held responsible under Article 7(1) for commission only. In this particular case we are dealing with the responsibility of the accused in relation to 12 different modes of criminal responsibility. The first one is planning. The second one is instigation. The third one is ordering. The fourth one is commission. The fifth one is joint criminal enterprise as an individual mode of commission. Six is aiding and abetting in planning, preparation or commission. Seven is aiding and abetting joint criminal enterprise. Eight is omission to prevent. Nine, failure to punish. Ten, co-perpetration. Eleven, indirect perpetration. And twelve, indirect co-perpetration. If we were to analyse the judgement under Rule 98 bis in Blagojevic, Jokic case, and if we wanted to formulate an indictment that would be a single incident indictment in relation to each mode of criminal responsibility, then we would, in relation to each of the accused individually, we would need to multiply 993 crimes with 12 modes of criminal responsibility, which would bring us to 11.916 counts of indictment in relation to each of the accused, or 71.496 counts of indictment in relation to all of them taken together. Does such an indictment discriminate against the accused in this case? Does such an indictment aggravate their defence cases? Those the questions that we believe we would provide answers to during these hearings under Rule 98 bis. I see that we have additional 15 minutes of time. I think that when we resume I will conclude with our proposals. In light on everything that we have stated so far, the Defence of General Petkovic proposes to the Trial Chamber the following: On the basis of Rule 54, the Trial Chamber should establish that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence do not allow for the possibility to have incidents joined within the same count of indictment, so that the indictment in which several count pertains to several incidents is formulated against the Rules, in violation of the Rules of Procedure. Second, we propose that the Trial Chamber establish that the rights of the accused may not depend on whether the Prosecutor would cover with one count of indictment one or several incidents, because otherwise that would mean the following: A, that one count of indictment pertains -- or, rather, if one count of indictment pertains to one incident, then the accused may be acquitted under Rule 98 bis from charges for that particular incident. However, if one count of indictment pertains to two incidents, then the accused may not be acquitted under Rule 98 bis from charges for the first incident, because the conditions were not met for him to be acquitted of the other incident within the same count of indictment. Our third proposal is as follows: Make it mandatory for the Prosecution to sever or separate incidents from one count of indictment and to formulate counts of indictment according to incidents as single-incident counts so that one count of indictment covers only one single incident. If this proposal should be accepted, then we suggest that hearings under Rule 98 bis be conducted after this new indictment is reformulated. We think that this manner of formulating an indictment is too complicated -- or, rather, if you believe that this is too complicated, we alternatively propose as follows: To allow the Prosecution not to change the indictment as it stands, to allow it to stand as a multi-incident indictment but, however, to establish that each count in this indictment is actually a multiple incident count, that each count actually represents a joinder of single-incident counts for the same crime so that the judgement under Rule 98 bis is handed down according to single incident counts which should be defined as such only within this trial -- for the purposes of this trial. If the Trial Chamber were to accept this proposal then the following would be achieved: All of the accused would be guaranteed the same rights regardless of the indictment was formulated in such a way to have one count cover one incident and or whether the indictment is formulated as multiple-incident count indictment. Second, what would be achieved is that the Trial Chamber would introduce the rules in formulating the indictment and would prevent the Prosecution from violating the Rules on Procedure and Evidence in creating the content of the indictment. Three, by doing so, the Trial Chamber would enable the Rule 98 bis to be applied in a manner which would protect fundamental human rights and freedoms, presumption of innocence, right to a fair trial, and right to a trial within a reasonable space of time. Four, such an application of Rule 98 bis would contribute to the entire trial being expeditious because the accused, or at least some of them, would be acquitted of certain charges which would reduce the total time needed in order to prepare and adduce evidence within the Defence case. We believe that the esteemed Trial Chamber will find sufficient time, will, and understanding to look into our proposal and to issue a decision which would make it clear that they believe that the rights of the accused before this Tribunal are not just declaratory and that they actually protect fundamental rights. If the Trial Chamber rejects our proposal then the Defence of General Petkovic [Realtime translation read in error "Perisic"] would like to invoke Rule 6(D) and require that it be allowed to file a petition under Rule 98 bis in accordance with the text of that provision which was in force when this trial was commenced. The Defence of General Petkovic would like to remind everyone that according to Rule 6(D) an amended Rule shall not operate to prejudice of rights of the accused or the convicted or acquitted person in any pending case. It is the opinion of everyone before this Court including the Judges of this Court that Rule 98 bis after its amendment in December of 2004 became a mere formality and then the rights of the accused to have an acquittal entered became significantly reduced, if not completely eliminated. We believe that there is no doubt that the new Rule, Rule 98 bis as formulated, jeopardises the rights of the accused to be acquitted in the situations when the Prosecution failed to prove their responsibility. This trial began some nine months before Rule 98 bis was amended. Therefore, according to Rule 6(D) the procedure under Rule 98 bis must be conducted in accordance with the Rule which was in force when this trial began. Your Honours, should you believe it necessary to rule on these issues as preliminary issues, then it would mean that we concluded with our presentation, but if you think that the Defence of General Petkovic can continue with its submissions under Rule 98 bis, then we shall continue. Should you like us to continue before my colleague Nicholas Stewart proceeds with explaining our case, I wish to say only the following: That the application -- or, rather, the submission of General Petkovic under Rule 98 bis will be based on the following: (A) that there is a possibility for the Trial Chamber to accept our proposal to amend the indictment in accordance with the rules on evidence and procedure which does not envisage the possibility of joining two or more incidents within the same count of indictment; or, that alternatively, in order to simplify the procedure, each incident within the same count of indictment should be treated as a separate count. The Defence of General Petkovic in that case will not challenge the jurisprudence in relation to failure to assess the credibility of witnesses and documentary evidence. We will not challenge the jurisprudence that an acquittal cannot be entered if the existing evidence cannot support at least one counts -- or one mode of criminal responsibility. Fourth, that joint criminal enterprise as a mode of criminal responsibility as applied here before this Tribunal affects any accused who held a high political, military, or other post, and brings it closer to the concept of strict criminal responsibility for membership in a criminal organisation. As a result of that, the mere fact that an accused held a high position is held to contain sufficient evidence on his responsibility for commission of crime -- crimes. This is the reason why the Defence would not request that an acquittal be entered due to lack of evidence on -- on responsibility of General Petkovic for modes of responsibility which have not been proven by a single piece of evidence for example in relation to planning, instigating, ordering, or direct personal perpetration. We shall ask that an acquittal be entered if for a particular crime there is no proof that all of the elements were met -- or, rather, there is no evidence that all of the elements exist, and if there is no evidence that such a crime occurred or took place as described in the indictment. I thank you, and now my colleague Mr. Stewart will take over. Your Honour, if I may correct a mistake on page 28, lines 14 and 15. It says General Pusic. It should say General Petkovic. We apologise both to General Pusic and General Petkovic for not registering that mistake on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I might use the two or three minutes that are left before the normal time when Your Honours take the break just to follow the last few remarks made by Ms. Alaburic as to where we are now and where we go. In effect, Ms. Alaburic has addressed the issue which we applied to be raised as a preliminary issue. One possibility, and we suggest it's actually got quite a lot to be said for it is that on that discrete issue, the Prosecution would naturally in accordance with normal fairness and procedure the Prosecution would have an opportunity to say whatever they wanted to say. Of course I leave open the possibility that other Defence teams might also have the opportunity. I'm in Your Honours' hands on that. And as Ms. Alaburic has indicated, if -- if we know where we are going then on that particular issue and in relation to the proposals which have been canvassed by Ms. Alaburic this afternoon, then -- well, we know what to do next. We know where to go next. We know what, if anything, to do next as far as our application is concerned, because that's entirely dependent on the ruling and clearly a ruling one way is going to mean that we -- well, we certainly save time. I don't want -- I want to make all submissions, of course, and Ms. Alaburic and I want to make all submissions which are relevant and potentially helpful to our client. What we don't want to do, though, is make absolutely futile submissions, waste our time, waste General Petkovic's time, waste the Court's time if they're simply going to end up as nothing at all because of the view that you take on this preliminary issue. So, Your Honour, I'm in Your Honours' hands, but we do suggest that the sensible thing is in fact to grapple with this issue and know where we are and that would be helpful to all and sundry and no doubt helpful to other Defence teams as well as the Prosecution and everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will summarise at my level if -- if I've understood, because to understand you, one needs to deepen what you have already said, but I think I understood that you had a preliminary issue concerning 98 bis, presenting a preliminary point articulated according to two elements. First element, you say that when this trial started Article 98 bis was drafted differently. It was a regime, that it was amended during the trial, and therefore for you it is the previous text of the rule which applies, and therefore those are the charges and not the counts. And the second element which you indicate is that you present a theory about joinder concerning counts, indicating that the indictment is in a certain way illegal because it puts at the door of the accused several crimes even sometimes for the same facts or events, and this is -- would be contrary to the Defence rights. You mentioned Canada, United States, Great Britain, and so on. Therefore, you are requesting the Chamber to decide and rule on what should be done. Now, on this preliminary issue, this will need, I think, from the Prosecution a response, because you have now started a new, completely new procedure which has never been attempted before about Article 98 bis, and I would like Mr. Scott to tell us what he thinks about it, and the Chamber indeed will deliberate to let you know what should be done about this. So, Mr. Scott, please, you have the floor. If you have understood, because it is rather involved, rather complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would ask since, again, of course as the Chamber knows there was no advance notice of any issue to be raised at these proceedings even though we asked for that, and since it is -- Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. That's -- no, that's extremely unfair. The advance notice was about a week or so ago when we made the application for the preliminary issue. It's been crystal clear that this issue was going to be raised and argued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no reason -- there's no reason for Mr. Stewart to get agitated. The Chamber will plainly recall that some days ago the Prosecution requested to be advised of the issues that would be raised in these 98 bis proceedings so that everyone, including the Prosecution and the Chamber and all parties could be adequately prepared to come into the courtroom. This issue, counsel's correct. There was some discussion about the scope of Rule 98 bis, but the Chamber at that point was quite adamant and has been adamant today that the current Rule would apply. Now, the Prosecution accepted that at face value. So that's where we are, and that's what I mean when I say, and there's no reason for Mr. Stewart to become excited about that. Now, this issue's now been raised. As the Chamber just said, it's a rather fundamental question attacking the entire viability of this procedure, and it is time for the break, and I would ask the Chamber that we take the break. The Prosecution will discuss this among ourselves and come back and make whatever further response we think we should make. It had been our hope, Your Honour, just since I'm on my feet, it had been our hope and anticipation that all the Defence arguments would be tendered at made all at once and the Prosecution would then make a response because, of course, there could be overlapping arguments, there could be interrelated arguments, and the Prosecution would rather make a response to all arguments at one time. So that would be our first preference, is that we take all arguments first, Defence arguments by all accused and the Prosecution will make its response at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not -- I'll let others judge whether the descriptions of agitated or excited apply, that seem to be very favourite words of Mr. Scott's. I'm simply going to try to do my job. But included in doing my job is to observe that, innocently no doubt, what Mr. Scott says - and I do say innocently - is in fact a misrepresentation of the exchange that took place on our application for preliminary issue, because it was perfectly clear that very helpful intervention made by His Honour Judge Trechsel at that time, which then led to a concerted view by the Trial Chamber was to the effect that, yes, this particular issue, the basis of which was made very clear on our application would be permitted to be canvassed on this application. There's never been the slightest indication we were resiling from that. The Prosecution have known for a week, or however long it is, that this point about the scope of 98 bis and whether it could apply to elements within a count as formulated in the indictment was absolutely clearly on the table as an issue, and to suggest that in any way it's taken them by surprise is simply false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will take a break at this point. We will deliberate during the 20 or 30 minutes, and then we will tell you what is decided after the break. Unless -- just a second, please. Unless Mr. Scott wishes to -- to take the floor to talk about the two major points that were raised by the Defence, the applicability of 6(D) with respect to 98 bis; and the second important point, the reformatting of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will take the floor, Your Honour, but I requested specifically to take it after the break, and I thought that was quite clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we shall take a break now. The Judges will deliberate during the break. We will listen to you, and we will take another break to deliberate. If I understood correctly, Ms. Alaburic and Mr. Stewart, they would like that the Chamber takes a decision, meaning that they would like the Chamber to render a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and I should start by saying good afternoon to you, Mr. President, and to each of the Judges, to all those in and around the courtroom. First, Your Honour, I -- I must note again, and I'm not saying this at all and my comment is not directed to Mr. Stewart at all, and I hope he will take that directly at face value. So there's no need to further address the point. My point is one of procedure and not as to Mr. Stewart or matter of personality. What has been raised this afternoon is a legal motion, a legal issue. If such a motion had been filed by -- raised by motion according to the rules, under the rules Prosecution would have two weeks to respond in writing to such a motion, and so I note that, Your Honour. Now, on this important legal issue, we're basically being required to respond to -- kind of off-the-cuff, as it were. Having said that, Your Honour, the Prosecution's responses would be twofold. First of all, Your Honour, much of what counsel has said on this issue is really goes to a challenge to the form of the indictment which under Rule 72 has to be brought prior to the time of trial. If the Chamber would like to look at Rule 72, preliminary motions being motions which (i) challenge jurisdiction; or (ii) allege defects in the form of the indictment; (iii) seek the severance of counts joined in one indictment under Rule 49 or seek separate trials under Rule 82(B), et cetera, are to be raised not later than 30 days after the disclosure of the supporting material. The very -- well, one -- certainly one of the reasons for that rule and I think similar rules in most systems and certainly true in the US federal system, is to avoid being exactly in this situation, that those kinds of motions have to be made very, very early in the process to avoid the waste of time and resources and energy by everyone. Saying that the count -- the indictment is not properly pled, saying that there are too many charges in one count, all of that is -- goes to Rule 72, and that motion should have been filed literally, literally, years ago. So we cannot, Your Honour, counsel -- with great respect, counsel cannot, via Rule 98 bis, move us backwards in time three years ago to a challenge to the form of indictment. The indictment -- number one. Number two, if for any reason the Chamber would be inclined to consider the form of the indictment, which we do not believe it should, with respect, then, Your Honour, I would submit -- the Prosecution would submit that the indictment in its current form is completely consistent with Tribunal jurisprudence and practice, not withstanding some of the examples given by counsel, and of course none of us in the courtroom, I don't think, have those -- certainly we don't, have any of those other indictments in front us. But my experience and observation would be that the form of indictment here, the way it is charged with multiple incidents being included in a particular count is the way that indictments have been brought for the past 15 years. That doesn't necessarily mean it's the only way or the best way, but that is the established practice and precedent of this Tribunal, and if now this one Trial Chamber is going to issue a ruling requiring that 15 years of practice be changed and the jurisprudence be changed, obviously that puts everyone, including the Prosecution, and for that matter, the Defence, at a substantial disadvantage. So that is the Rule 72 issue, and we submit that most of what counsel has tendered or argued is really an attempt under Rule 72 to attack the form of the indictment. Those motions -- any such motions were made years ago and ruled on years ago, and under Rule 72 cannot be raised at this time. In terms of the 6(D) issue, Your Honour, we would note a couple of things. First of all, the amended Rule 98 bis does not change the substantive standard. The standards as -- at least some of which counsel read out. The standard to be applied has not changed. Therefore, there can be no prejudice from a change in the Rule based on that. There is no prejudice flowing from the change in December 2004 since the legal standard to be applied did not change. At most, what has changed is the procedure to be followed, not the stand order to be applied. And we would submit on that point, Your Honour, as I think in -- I won't say all systems, but at least in a good many systems, I think, and certainly in the US system, there is a distinction drawn between procedural changes -- procedural legal and substantive law. Of course, you can't create ex post facto crimes and charge a crime -- change in the law to charge a crime that wasn't a crime before. This is a purely procedural matter. The legal standard itself has not changed and, therefore, the Prosecution submits that Rule 6(D) is not implicated by this. Finally, Your Honour, if the Chamber were despite all of those arguments inclined to apply Rule 6(D) in this case, then the Prosecution would submit with great respect, it would put us in a position of indeed going back to the entire previous procedure of extensive written submissions, probably 3 or 400-page briefs and some weeks of preparation. You can't have it both ways. If we're going back in time, if we're going to go back to the old days, then the old days have to apply, and both the Defence and the Prosecution will have to prepare its extensive, detailed submissions to that effect. But we can't have it both ways. We can't have -- we're going to go back the old way but then we're going to do it all on the fly standing on our feet in the courtroom. So the Chamber can decide if it wishes to do so what practice they want to follow. But it's our submission, Your Honour, number one, this is a Rule 72 issue. This motion could and should have been made a long time ago if it goes to the form of the indictment how the offences are charged, and that has long been resolved and is over -- is overdue and that right has expired. Number two, under Rule 6(D) we do not believe there has in fact been any substantial prejudice to the Defence. The standard to be applied has not changed. It is at most a procedural change and does not -- therefore, we do not believe it raises -- rises to the level of substantive prejudice to the accused. And again our third point, Your Honour, in summary is if the Chamber were to accept that argument, then the Prosecution ask to be -- the entire process to be rescheduled and reformatted so that we return to the previous practice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I'd like the right to reply. I consider this to be necessary with respect to the first objection made by my learned friend, Mr. Scott, relating to the assertion that objections to the form of the indictment should have been done in preliminary submissions when it came to the form of the indictment pursuant to Rule 72. The Defence of General Petkovic completely agrees with Mr. Scott that it is the topic of objection to the form of the indictment, that that's what that deals with, but I'd like to remind you of the following fact: At the point in time when the Defence teams prepared their objections to the form of the indictment, what was in force was the old Rule 98 [Realtime transcript read in error "92"] bis, and at that point in time not a single objective reason existed for the Defence to consider that by a joinder of a number of indictments in one count of the indictment the right of the accused would in any way be reduced, diminished. It was only after the fact that Rule 98 bis was amended and after jurisprudence and case law showed how it was to be applied could we possibly have reason with the necessary explanations to object to the form of the indictment, but at the time all the time limits for doing that had expired. Now, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me if I ask, because I do not understand it seems. The amended indictment is dated 16 November 2005, and the Rules were changed in December 2004. So it would seem to me that almost one year after the Rules had been changed it would have been possible to refer to the changed Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I be allowed to remind you that we did object to the first indictment and that it was on the basis of those objections that the amended indictment was issued. The deadline for submitting objections to the indictment pursuant to Rule 72 was the 15th of December, 2004. So that was 2004. And that was the day when the amended text of Rule 98 bis -- let me repeat, 92 bis, for the record, anyway, this came into force on that day, and the Defence teams had completed their submissions and tabled them to this Tribunal. So the amended Rule 98 bis came into force after the Defence teams objected to the form of the indictment and issues of jurisdiction. So in keeping with the ruling of the Tribunal, the -- there was an amended indictment by the Prosecution, and once an indictment is amended, the Defence has the right to repeat their objections to the form only with respect to the new counts, new charges, in actual fact. So it is the position of this court that in the amended indictment there were no new charges. So our additional requests for objection to the indictment were rejected. Therefore, I wanted to continue with my explanation. It is possible during the proceedings the Rules can be amended in such a way that an element from the form of the indictment really does become a factor for the Defence and that the deadlines have expired a long time ago, which means that the Defence has lost its right to retroactively oppose the an application of some Rule which means the elimination or diminishment of an element or right. And we therefore consider that, first of all, when we tabled our objections to the form of the indictment that the topic of multiple-incident count was not one that was important from a single right of the accused before this Tribunal. We launched this topic on the -- at the first opportunity when it was seen that this subject could be important for realising the rights of the accused, and that is the application of Rule 92 bis precisely -- 98 bis precisely, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout it says 92 bis in the record. I'm talking about 98 bis, 98 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to correct and state for the record and partly in response to Judge Trechsel's question, the preliminary motions were filed in this case beginning on the 15th of December, 2004, and the Rule was enacted on the 8th of December, 2004. Now, not to split -- not to split hairs too much, but the Rule was in effect at the time that the preliminary motions were filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we're wrong in the interpretation, but according to the information we have and data, the Rule was amended on the 8th of December, 2004, that is true, and in conformity with Rule 6(D) [Realtime transcript read in error "60"], it came into effect six [as interpreted] days after it was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I follow on to what my colleague Ms. Alaburic has just said? In reading Rule 6, the second part and the sentence: "That shall not -- but shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused or of a convicted or acquitted person in any pending case." For us to respond to this question that has just been raised during the day as to what happened before, pending case in this specific case we should know at what point in time during the proceedings and according to the Rules we define this moment of launching criminal proceedings. As we know in different jurisdictions this is different. It could be, but the Rules don't have any specific provision on this at least as far as I know, and I don't think I'm wrong. As I said it could be the date when the indictment was confirmed, but it could also be the day when the accused appeared in court for the first time before the Trial Chamber. But both dates were during the enforcement of the old Rule 98 bis. So we're not counting the amended indictment which came at the very end, because we in fact had three indictments, unless I'm very much mistaken. The last amendment is the questionable one. If before that we establish on what day -- or, rather, what day we consider the proceedings to have been launched and that the proceedings are pending, the case is pending, then we cannot decide what came before and what came after. We consider that it is obvious, because of the previous indictment, the appearance of the accused in court that quite obviously the proceedings were already under way. That is to say, after the 4th -- or, rather, after the 8th of December when the new amendment came into force. And as my colleague said it came into force eight days after it was published. Just to not have to take the floor again I can continue now. I think Mr. Scott is claiming that there is no essential difference between the new and the old Rule 98 bis. I don't think that I should present any special arguments on that score but I would like to point out three details. The old Rule gives the right proprio motu for the Trial Chamber to make a judgement in this stage, whereas according to the new Rule the Trial Chamber cannot do that until it evokes parts of Rule 54, but not on the basis of Rule 98 bis. The second important difference is that according to the old Rule, the Defence should make their submissions in writing. That's a big difference because we all know from our experience that if you have something done in writing it is easier to follow and more precise than oral submissions, if we take into account the speed at which the speaker is speaking, the interpretation and so on and so forth. And further the most important and significant difference is that according to the old Rule you could -- one or more offences charged in the indictment. That was necessary. So in the way the technique applied by the Prosecution in defining the counts of the indictment we could address the counts of the indictment successfully if it was a part of the count, and in our indictment the description of an event in a certain paragraph which does not exist in this new Rule. So without a doubt the differences are great and I cannot agree with the position taken by the Prosecution that there are very few differences or negligible differences between the old Rule 98 bis and the new one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I might be allowed to put right two errors on page 47, line 2. I was speaking about Rule 6(D) and not Rule 60, and I also said that it came into force within a space of seven days and not six days. And may I also present additional arguments with respect to what my colleague Mr. Kovacic said in comparing the texts of the two Rule 98 bis.
